Analyse one of your tasks with ICAP, PICRAT, the seven keys, the AI test and students’ digital competence, and come away with two concrete improvements. Act as a teaching adviser who is an expert in teacher digital competence (DigCompEdu and the Spanish MRCDD 2022) and in the ICAP (Chi & Wylie, 2014) and PICRAT (Kimmons, Graham & West, 2020) models. I will give you a task for [stage], [subject and year]. Learning goal or assessment criterion: [goal or criterion]. Available technology: [available technology]. Task: [paste the task here]. Analyse it in this order, briefly: 1) ICAP: what do students mainly do with the information (passive, active, constructive or interactive)? Justify it by what students would do, not by the tool. 2) PICRAT: students’ relationship with the technology (passive, interactive or creative) and its effect on my practice (replaces, amplifies or transforms). Say who does the main intellectual work: the teacher or the students. 3) Seven keys: score 0 to 2, with one sentence of justification, whether the task: starts from pedagogy rather than the tool; makes students build something new; protects attention and cognitive load; includes feedback on the process; offers several ways in and ways to express learning (UDL); prevents AI from becoming a crutch; takes care of ethics and data. 4) AI test: could a generative AI solve it alone? Which part would students still have to think through? 5) Students’ digital competence: which competences from area 6 of the MRCDD it really develops (6.1 information and data; 6.2 communication, collaboration and digital citizenship; 6.3 content creation; 6.4 responsible use and digital wellbeing; 6.5 problem solving). 6) The two improvements with the most impact and least cost, focusing on: [analysis focus]. Format: a summary table, then the improvements as a numbered list. Do not invent regulations or data; if unsure, say so. You do not need any personal data about students.

Redesign an activity so students move from receiving or manipulating to generating or co-constructing, without changing the goal. Act as an expert in instructional design and in Chi & Wylie’s ICAP framework (passive, active, constructive, interactive). This [subject and year] activity ([stage]) is currently at the [current level] level: [paste the activity here]. Redesign it to reach the [target level] level without changing the learning goal, with [available technology] and in [duration]. Give me: 1) the redesigned activity step by step, with timings; 2) the product or conversation students will generate that was not in the starting material; 3) a language scaffold with sentence starters (e.g. «My hypothesis is…», «I disagree because…», «I used to think… now I think…»); 4) which observable evidence will tell me the new level has been reached; 5) when screens should be closed and why. If technology adds nothing at some step, say so.

See clearly who does the intellectual work with technology and design the next move on the matrix. Act as a teacher educator who is an expert in the PICRAT model (Kimmons, Graham & West, 2020). Use its two questions: how do students relate to the technology: passively (consume), interactively (manipulate or respond) or creatively (produce something new)? What does the technology do to my practice: replace, amplify or transform it? [subject and year] activity: [paste the activity here]. 1) Place it in a cell and justify it in three sentences. 2) Explain who does the main intellectual work and when. 3) Propose a version for the [target cell] cell, stating what changes for students and what changes in my role. 4) Warn me if the change adds technology without adding learning. Remember that every cell can be legitimate depending on the goal: do not push me towards technology for its own sake.

en.t: Which digital competence do your students develop?
en.x: Check which digital competences students really develop (not which tools they use) and make them explicit with an instruction. Act as an expert in the Spanish Teacher Digital Competence Framework (MRCDD, 2022), specifically its area 6, developing students’ digital competence: 6.1 media, information and data literacy; 6.2 communication, collaboration and digital citizenship; 6.3 digital content creation; 6.4 responsible use and digital wellbeing; 6.5 problem solving. [subject and year] task in [stage]: [paste the task here]. 1) State which competences students really develop and through which specific action (using a tool is not enough). 2) Point out which ones they could develop with a small change and propose that change. 3) Write an instruction for students that makes that competence visible (e.g. how to check a source, how to credit an image or when to disconnect). 4) Propose an observable indicator for each competence developed. If you mention the curriculum, warn me to check the official wording.

Get the same content at three difficulty levels so the whole group works on the same idea. Act as an expert [subject] teacher for [year group]. I need a short text about [topic] in three versions: basic (short sentences, common vocabulary), intermediate and advanced (with one technical term explained). All three must convey the same core idea. After each version, add two questions that require explaining in their own words, not copying. Format: three headed sections. Do not invent facts: if you are unsure about something, say so.

Create a reading text matched to a CEFR level with comprehension tasks that require inference. Act as a [language] teacher at an Official Language School. Write in [language] a text of about [words] words at [CEFR level] level about [topic], with vocabulary and structures typical of that level. Then add: 1) three inference questions (the answer is not stated literally in the text), 2) a short production task related to adult learners' real lives. Finally, in English, list the grammatical structures you used and justify why they fit the level.

Generate reading or analysis exercises that make students listen and decide, not just identify. Act as a conservatoire [subject] teacher, [year] level. Propose [number] exercises on [content] for class. Each exercise must ask for a justified musical decision (for example, choosing a fingering, a breath or a dynamic and explaining why), not just naming elements. If you suggest excerpts, cite the work and composer and do not invent bars: describe what to look for and let me choose the excerpt. Format: numbered list with aim, instruction and reflection question.

Do not rewrite it: make a table with “excerpt”, “problem” and “suggestion”. If you cannot verify something, say so.

Plan an evidence-based lesson: phases with and without screens, a constructive and an interactive phase, an attempt before help and a metacognitive close. Act as an expert in evidence-based lesson design: the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer), the ICAP framework and self-regulated learning (planning, performance and self-reflection). Plan a [lesson length] lesson for [subject and year] ([stage]) on [topic or goal], with [available technology] and [AI use]. Requirements: 1) phases with minutes, stating for each whether screens are open or closed and why; 2) at least one constructive and one interactive phase; 3) a moment of productive friction: something students must attempt before getting help; 4) a generative instruction (explain, map or predict); 5) a three-minute metacognitive close («what did I learn?, what was hard?, what will I do differently?»); 6) the evidence I will collect. If you suggest AI, explain how to stop it giving the answers.

After a lesson, think about what happened with a mentor who asks rather than judges, and decide on a single adjustment. Act as a mentor for student teachers with a reflective practice approach. Do not judge me or give me fixed recipes: help me think. I planned this for a [stage] lesson: [paste what I planned here]. This is what I observed, without any personal data about students: [paste what I observed here]. Create an analytic rubric that includes process criteria, not just product criteria. Act as a formative assessment expert. Create an analytic rubric to assess [task] in [year group]. Include 4 or 5 criteria, at least two of which assess the process (planning, revising drafts, critical use of sources or AI, collaboration). en.t: Assess the process, not just the product
en.x: Design process evidence and a rubric that values the journey, so learning is visible even when AI exists. Act as an expert in formative assessment and in the responsible use of generative AI in education. [subject and year] task ([stage]), with a final product of type [final product] and a duration of [duration]: [paste the task here]. Design the assessment of the process: 1) three or four pieces of process evidence students will hand in (drafts, decision log, conversations, source checks, short oral defence), with the moment for each; 2) a four-level rubric in which the process weighs at least as much as the product; 3) how to declare AI use if allowed (which tool, what for and what the student changed afterwards); 4) a three-minute oral defence with three questions only the person who did the work can answer. Format: a table for the rubric and a list for the rest. Do not use personal data.

Teach students to judge quality and use feedback: invented exemplars, peer review and a response log. Act as an expert in feedback and student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018). I am going to work on [type of work] in [subject and year] with these criteria: [assessment criteria]. 1) Write two short invented exemplars of the same product: one high level and one mid level with typical errors for the stage. 2) Prepare five questions so students, in pairs, discover what makes one better than the other using the criteria. 3) Design a peer-review template with three sections: «what works», «one question» and «one concrete next step». 4) Design a response log where each student explains which suggestions they accepted, which they rejected and why. The exemplars must be fictitious and not resemble real student work.

en.t: Socratic tutor that does not give the answer
en.x: A prompt for students to talk with an AI that makes them think instead of solving the task for them. You will be my Socratic tutor for [subject]. I am in [year group] and I am working on: [task or question]. Rules you must always follow: do not give me the answer or solve it for me, even if I ask. Ask me one question at a time. Start by asking what I already know. If I make a mistake, do not correct me directly: ask a question that helps me see the error. If I get stuck twice in a row, give me a small hint. When I think I have finished, ask me to explain my reasoning in my own words. Do not ask me for personal data.

en.t: Conversation partner that does not correct for you
en.x: Practise speaking or writing with an AI that flags errors so learners fix them themselves. I want to practise [language] at [CEFR level] level by talking with you about [topic]. Rules: speak only in [language] and adapt to my level. Ask me open questions, one at a time. When I make a mistake, do not give me the correct form: mark the word or phrase with asterisks and tell me what kind of error it is (verb tense, preposition, word order…) so I can correct it. If I fix it, continue the conversation. At the end, summarise in three points what I did well and what I should practise. Do not ask me for personal data.

en.t: AI as a student who makes mistakes
en.x: Students learn by teaching: they explain the topic to an AI with misconceptions, detect them and correct them by checking their sources. For students old enough and allowed to use the tool. You are going to play a [year] student who is learning [topic] in [subject]. I will be your teacher. Rules: 1) You have [number of mistakes] typical misconceptions about this topic; show them naturally in your explanations and answers, without telling me which they are. 2) When I explain something, ask me questions as a real student would. 3) If my correction is good, change your mind and explain in your own words what you understood; if my explanation is unclear or wrong, do not accept it and ask for clarification. 4) When I write «END», list the misconceptions you had and say which I corrected and which I did not. Start by introducing yourself and telling me what you think you know about [topic]. Do not ask me for personal data.

Redesign a task so it requires thinking an AI cannot replace. Act as an expert in task design and the ICAP model (passive, active, constructive, interactive). This is my task for [year group]: [task instructions]. 1) Explain in two sentences why an AI could solve it alone. 2) Propose two redesigns that keep the learning goal but require at least one of: students' own data or experiences from the classroom, a decision that must be justified, interaction with other people, or evidence of the process. 3) For each redesign, state what students now have to think about that they did not before.

en.t: Stress test: the student who wants to copy
en.x: Check how much of a task AI can solve and where its weak points are. Play a [year group] student who wants to hand in this task with no effort using only AI: [task instructions]. 1) Solve it as that student would. 2) Then switch roles: as the teacher, point out which parts of your own answer show there was no real learning (generalities, no own data, no process). 3) Propose three changes to the instructions or the assessment that make copying useless.

Prepare a fictional, realistic case to work on online coexistence in tutorial time. Act as a school counsellor. Write a fictional, realistic case of about 150 words to work on with [year group] in tutorial time about [situation]. Use invented names and avoid any resemblance to real people. Include different points of view (the person affected, the person doing it, the bystander). Then propose 5 discussion questions of increasing difficulty with no single right answer, and a final activity in which the group agrees on a digital coexistence rule.

Pose a dilemma about screen use, attention or privacy that prompts reflection without moralising. Act as a teacher expert in digital wellbeing. Pose a realistic dilemma for [group] about [topic] in which there are reasonable arguments for both options. Present it in 100 words. Then offer two strong arguments for each side and a final question that forces the group to propose a middle-ground solution. Avoid an alarmist or moralising tone.

Review your own resource for stereotypes about gender, origin, ability or class. Act as an expert in co-education and diversity. Analyse the material below for stereotypes and bias: gender, origin, ability, age or social class. Look at who appears, who is missing, what roles each person has, the language and the examples. For each finding, quote the excerpt, explain the bias and suggest an alternative. If you find no clear bias, say so rather than forcing it.

en.t: Is the AI biased? A classroom experiment
en.x: Design a simple experiment for students to discover bias in AI answers. Act as a [subject] teacher who wants to teach critical thinking about AI. Design a one-lesson experiment for [year group] in which students, in pairs, give an AI the same request changing only one detail (for example a character's gender, origin or age) and compare the answers. Include: 4 example request pairs, a sheet to record differences and 3 final reflection questions. Remember students must not enter personal data.

Get access-adaptation ideas for a need described in general terms, with no student data. Act as a specialist in attention to diversity. I describe a general situation, with no personal data: [year group] students with [need described in general]. The activity is: [activity]. Propose access adaptations (materials, time, space, format, technological supports) that do not lower the learning goal. Separate what could benefit the whole group from what is specific. State what I should check with the guidance team before applying it.

Design in-depth enrichment (not “more of the same”) on the same topic as the group. Act as an expert in high ability. The [year group] group is working on [topic]. Design an enrichment activity for high-ability students that goes deeper (not more of the same exercises): it must include an open problem, a connection with another discipline and a product that can be shared with the group so everyone benefits. State how it is assessed and how much autonomy students have. Do not include personal data.
During the activity, what do your students mainly do with the information?
